''distichum''|volume=2|last=Watson|first=Frank D.|access-date=28 September 2024}}</ref> '''bald cypress''', '''swamp cypress'''; {{langx|fr|cyprès chauve}};
''cipre'' in [[Louisiana_French|Louisiana]]) is a [[deciduous]] [[Pinophyta|conifer]] in the family [[Cupressaceae]]. It is native to the [[Southeastern United States]]. Hardy and tough, this tree adapts to a wide range of soil types, whether wet, salty, dry, or swampy. It is noted for the russet-red fall color of its lacy needles. It is both extremely flood tolerant and rather drought hardy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bald cypress |url=https://www.butler.k-state.edu/horticulture/agent-articles/trees-and-shrubs/baldcypruss/ |access-date=2026-06-14 |website=K-State Extension Butler County |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> 

This plant has some cultivated varieties<ref>{{PLANTS |id=TADI2 |taxon=Taxodium distichum |access-date=8 December 2015}}</ref><ref name="farjon">Farjon, A. (2005). ''Monograph of Cupressaceae and Sciadopitys''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. {{ISBN|1-84246-068-4}}</ref><ref name="fna">{{eFloras|1|200005404|Taxodium distichum |family=Cupressaceae |first=Frank D. |last=Watson}}</ref><ref name="gd">{{Gymnosperm Database |family=Cupressaceae |genus=Taxodium |species=distichum |subspecies=distichum}}</ref><ref name="Silvics">{{Silvics |volume=1 |genus=Taxodium |species=distichum |first1=L. P. |last1=Wilhite |first2=J. R. |last2=Toliver}}</ref> and is often used in groupings in public spaces. Common names include bald cypress, swamp cypress, white cypress, tidewater red cypress, gulf cypress, and red cypress.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mortonarb.org/trees-plants/tree-plant-descriptions/bald-cypress|title=Bald-cypress {{!}} The Morton Arboretum|website=www.mortonarb.org|access-date=2019-01-14}}</ref><ref name="arborday.org">{{Cite web|url=https://www.arborday.org/trees/treeguide/treedetail.cfm?itemID=787|title=Baldcypress Tree on the Tree Guide at arborday.org|website=www.arborday.org|access-date=2019-01-15}}</ref>

The bald cypress was designated the official [[list of U.S. state trees|state tree]] of [[Louisiana]] in 1963.<ref name=":6">{{cite book|title=Louisiana Almanac, 2006-2007|page=431|last1=Calhoun|first1=Milburn|last2=Frois|first2=Jeanne|isbn=978-1-58980-307-7|publisher=Pelican Publishing|edition=17th|date=31 May 2006}}</ref>

Bald cypress trees are valued because of their rot-resistant heartwood when the trees are mature. Because of this, the trees are often used for making fence posts, doors, flooring, caskets, and a number of other items. 

==Description==
[[File:Cypress buttresses.jpg|thumb|left|Cypress grove in winter]]

''Taxodium distichum'' is a large, slow to fast-growing,<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=ENH-778/ST620: Taxodium distichum: Baldcypress |url=https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/ST620 |access-date=2026-04-16 |website=Ask IFAS - Powered by EDIS |language=en}}</ref> and long-lived [[tree]]. It typically grows to heights of {{convert|35|-|120|ft|-1}} and has a [[Diameter at breast height|trunk diameter]] of {{convert|3|-|7|ft|1}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Trees: South Florida and the Keys|others=Koeser, Andrew K.; Friedman, Melissa H.; Hasing, Gitta; Franck, Alan R.; Finley, Holly; Schelb, Julie |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-68340-015-8 |location=Gainesville, FL|pages=296–7|oclc=962233681|last1 = Koeser|first1 = Andrew K.|last2 = Friedman|first2 = Melissa H. |last3 = Hasing|first3 = Gitta|last4 = Franck|first4 = Alan R.|last5 = Finley|first5 = Holly|last6 = Schelb|first6 = Julie}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nwf.org/Home/Educational-Resources/Wildlife-Guide/Plants-and-Fungi/Bald-Cypress|title=Bald Cypress|website=National Wildlife Federation|language=en|access-date=2019-01-21}}</ref>

The main trunk is often surrounded by [[cypress knee]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|first=George K|last=Rogers|title=Bald Cypress knees, Taxodium distichum (Cupressaceae): An anatomical study, with functional implications|journal=Flora|volume=278|year=2021|article-number=151788|doi=10.1016/j.flora.2021.151788}}</ref> The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is grayish brown to reddish brown, thin, and fibrous with a stringy texture. Young trees have more easily-peelable bark.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/taxodium-distichum/|title=Taxodium distichum|work=North Carolina Plant Toolbox|publisher=North Carolina State University|access-date=2026-08-25}}</ref>

The needle-like [[leaves]] are {{convert|1/2|to|3/4|in|cm}} long and are simple, alternate, green, and linear, with entire margins. In autumn, the leaves turn yellow or copper red.<ref name=":0" /> The bald cypress is deciduous.<ref name=":2" />

This species is [[monoecious]], with male and female cones on a single plant forming on slender, tassel-like structures near the edge of branchlets. The tree produces cones in April and the seeds ripen in October.<ref name=":0" /> The male and female [[strobili]] are produced from buds formed in late autumn, with pollination in early winter, and mature in about 12 months. Male [[Conifer cone|cones]] emerge on [[panicle]]s that are {{convert|4|–|5|in|cm}} inches long. Female cones are round, [[resin]]ous and green while young. They then turn hard and then brown as the tree matures. They are globular and {{convert|2.0|-|3.5|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} in diameter. They have from 20 to 30 spirally arranged, four-sided scales, each bearing one, two, or rarely three triangular [[seed]]s. Each cone contains 20 to 40 large seeds. The cones disintegrate at maturity to release the seeds. The seeds are {{convert|5|–|10|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} long, the largest of any species of [[Cupressaceae]], and are produced every year, with heavy crops every 3–5 years. The seedlings have three to nine, but usually six, [[cotyledon]]s each.<ref name="farjon" />

[[File:The "Senator" bald cypress tree.jpg|thumb|The "Senator" bald cypress tree]]

The bald cypress grows in full sunlight to partial shade; it grows best in wet or well-drained soil, but can tolerate dry soil. It is moderately able to grow in [[aerosol]]s of salt water. It does well in acid, neutral, and alkaline soils across the full range of light (sandy), medium (loamy), and heavy (clay) soils. It can also grow in saline soils. It can tolerate atmospheric pollution. The cones are often consumed by wildlife.<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://www.arborday.org/trees/treeguide/treedetail.cfm?itemID=787|title=Baldcypress Tree on the Tree Guide at arborday.org |website= www.arborday.org |access-date=2019-01-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url= https://www.srs.fs.usda.gov/pubs/misc/ag_654/volume_1/taxodium/distichum.htm |title=Taxodium distichum (L|website=www.srs.fs.usda.gov|access-date=2019-01-15}} {{USDA}}</ref>

The tallest known specimen, near [[Williamsburg, Virginia]], is 44.11 m (145 ft) tall.<ref name="gd" /> The National Champion Bald Cypress is recognized as the largest member of its species in the country and is listed as such on the [[National Register of Champion Trees]] by American Forest. The National Champion Bald Cypress is in the [[Cat Island National Wildlife Refuge]], near [[St. Francisville, Louisiana]], and it is {{convert|96|feet}} tall, {{convert|56|feet}} in circumference, and is estimated to be approximately 1,500 years old. The oldest known living specimen, found along the [[Black River (North Carolina)|Black River]] in [[North Carolina]], is at least 2,624 years old, rendering it the oldest living tree in eastern [[North America]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Longevity, climate sensitivity, and conservation status of wetland trees at Black River, North Carolina |journal=Environmental Research Communications |volume=1 |issue=4 |page=041002 |doi=10.1088/2515-7620/ab0c4a|year=2019|last1=Stahle|first1=D. W.|last2=Edmondson|first2=J. R. |last3=Howard |first3=I. M. |last4=Robbins |first4=C. R.|last5=Griffin|first5=R. D.|last6=Carl|first6=A.|last7=Hall|first7=C. B. |last8=Stahle |first8=D. K. |last9=Torbenson |first9=M. C. A.|bibcode=2019ERCom...1d1002S |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

[[The Senator (tree)|The Senator]], a bald cypress in [[Longwood, Florida]], was {{convert|165|feet}} tall before the hurricane of 1925, when it lost about {{convert|40|feet}} in height. It had a circumference of {{convert|47|feet}} and a diameter of {{convert|17.5|feet}} and was estimated to be 3,500 years old. It was burned down accidentally in 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-02-29 |title="Burn In Hell": Facebook Users Attack Woman Arrested For Fire That Killed 3,500-Year-Old Cypress Tree |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/the-senator-burns-fire-sara-barnes-arrested_n_1308513 |access-date=2023-02-14 |website=HuffPost |language=en}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The closely related ''[[Taxodium ascendens]]'' (pond cypress) is treated by some botanists as a distinct species,<ref name=usda>{{PLANTS |symbol=TADI2 |taxon=Taxodium distichum}}</ref><ref>{{PLANTS |symbol=TAAS |taxon=Taxodium ascendens}}</ref> while others classify it as merely a [[variety (botany)|variety]] of bald cypress,<ref name=farjon/><ref name=gd/> as ''Taxodium distichum'' var. ''imbricatum'' (Nutt.) Croom. It differs in shorter leaves borne on erect shoots, and in ecology, being largely confined to low-nutrient [[blackwater river|blackwater]] habitats. A few authors also treat ''[[Taxodium mucronatum]]'' as a variety of bald cypress, as ''T. distichum'' var. ''mexicanum'' Gordon, thereby considering the genus as comprising only one species.<ref name=fna1>{{eFloras|1|132353|Taxodium |family=Cupressaceae |first=Frank D. |last=Watson}}</ref> 

==Habitat and distribution==
[[Image:Bald Cypress.JPG|thumb|Bald cypress in [[Trap Pond State Park]], [[Delaware]]]]
[[File:Caddo Lake- Cypress.jpg|thumb|right|Bald cypress on the [[Texas]] side of [[Caddo Lake]]]]

The native range extends from southeastern [[New Jersey]] south to [[Florida]] and west to Central [[Texas]] and southeastern [[Oklahoma]], and also inland up the [[Mississippi River]] to southernmost [[Illinois]] and [[Indiana]]. Ancient bald cypress [[forest]]s, with some trees more than 1,700 years old, once dominated [[swamp]]s in the Southeast. The original range had been thought to only reach as far north as [[Delaware]], but researchers have now found a natural forest on the [[Cape May]] Peninsula in southern New Jersey. The species can also be found growing outside its natural native range, in [[New York (state)|New York]] and [[Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":0" /> 

The largest remaining [[Old-growth forest|old-growth]] stands are at [[Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary]], near [[Naples, Florida]], and in the Three Sisters tract along eastern North Carolina's [[Black River (North Carolina)|Black River]]. The Corkscrew trees are around 500 years of age, and some exceed {{Convert|40|m|abbr=on}} in height. In 1985, the Black River trees were cored by a [[dendrochronologist]] from the [[University of Arkansas]], who found that some began growing as early as 364'' ''AD.  A subsequent visit to the area in 2019 revealed a tree dated by its tree-ring count to 605'' ''BC, ranking as the ninth-oldest tree in the world.<ref>{{cite web
   |url=http://www.pocosinpress.com/Methuselah.pdf
   |title=Searching for Methuselah
   |pages=1–3
   |author=Paul Ferguson
   |year=2008
   |publisher=Pocosin Press
   |access-date=21 April 2011
   |archive-date=23 March 2012
   |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323102656/http://www.pocosinpress.com/Methuselah.pdf
   }}</ref> 
[[File:Bald Cypress (Taxodium distichum) growing on the Guadalupe River, Kerr County, Texas, USA (14 April 2012).jpg|thumb|Bald cypress (''Taxodium distichum'') growing near the western extreme of its range on the Guadalupe River in the semi-arid [[Edwards Plateau]], Kerr County, Texas (14 April 2012)]]In 2012, [[scuba diver]]s discovered an [[Submerged forest|underwater cypress forest]] several miles off the coast of [[Mobile, Alabama]], in 60 feet of water. The forest contains trees that could not be dated with [[radiocarbon dating|radiocarbon methods]], indicating that they are more than 50,000 years old and thus most likely lived in the early glacial interval of the last ice age. The cypress forest is well preserved, and when samples are cut, they still smell like fresh cypress. A team, which has not yet published its results in a peer-reviewed journal, is studying the site. One possibility is that [[Hurricane Katrina]] exposed the grove of bald cypress, which had been protected under ocean floor sediments.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.livescience.com/37977-underwater-cypress-forest-discovered.html|title=Primeval Underwater Forest Discovered in Gulf of Mexico|date=8 July 2013|publisher=Live Science|access-date=15 January 2019}}</ref>

==Reproduction and early growth==
[[File:2014-11-02 14 12 30 Bald Cypress foliage during autumn along Hunters Ridge Drive in Hopewell Township, New Jersey.jpg|thumb|right|Foliage in autumn just before shedding]]
The bald cypress is [[monoecious]]. Male and female strobili mature in one growing season from buds formed the previous year. The male catkins are about {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter and are borne in slender, purplish, drooping clusters {{convert|7|to|13|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long that are conspicuous during the winter on this deciduous conifer. Pollen is shed in March and April. Female conelets are found singly or in clusters of two or three. The globose cones turn from green to brownish-purple as they mature from October to December. The cones are {{convert|13|to|36|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter and consist of 9 to 15 four-sided scales that break away irregularly after maturity. Each scale can bear two (rarely three) irregular, triangular seeds with thick, horny, warty coats and projecting flanges.<ref>Faulkner, Stephen P. 1982. Genetic variation of cones, seed and nursery-grown seedlings of baldcypress [Taxodium distichum (L.) Rich.] provenances. M.S. Thesis, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge. 71 p.</ref><ref name="Radford, Albert E. 1968">Radford, Albert E., Harry E. Ahles, and C. Ritchie Bell. 1968. Manual of the vascular flora of the Carolinas. University of North Carolina Press, Chapel Hill. 1183 p.</ref><ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1965">U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service. 1965. Silvics of forest trees of the United States. H. A. Fowells, comp. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agriculture Handbook 271. Washington, DC. 762 p.</ref><ref name="Silvics"/><ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1974">U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service. 1974. Seeds of woody plants in the United States. C. S. Schopmeyer, tech. coord. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agriculture Handbook 450. Washington, DC. 883 p.</ref> The number of seeds per cone averages 16 and ranges from 2 to 34. Cleaned seeds number from about 5,600 to 18,430 per kg (2,540 to 8,360 per lb).<ref name="Silvics"/><ref name="Radford, Albert E. 1968"/><ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1965"/><ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1974"/>

===Seed production and dissemination===
Some seeds are produced every year, and good seed crops occur at three- to five-year intervals.<ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1974"/> At maturity, the cone scales with their resin-coated seeds adhering to them, or sometimes entire cones, drop to the water or ground.<ref>Stubbs, Jack. 1983. Personal communication. USDA Forest Service, Southeastern Forest Experiment Station, Clemson, SC.</ref> This drop of mature seeds is often hastened by squirrels, which eat bald cypress seeds, but usually drop several scales with undamaged seeds still attached to each cone they pick.<ref>Brunswig, Norman L. 1983. Personal communication. National Audubon Society, Francis Beidler Forest, Harleyville, SC.</ref> Floodwaters spread the scales or cones along streams and are the most important means of seed dissemination.<ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1965"/>

===Seedling development===
[[File:Bald Cypress swamp and Spanish Moss.jpg|thumb|Bald cypress swamp and Spanish moss at First Landing State Park in Virginia Beach, Virginia]]
[[Germination]] is [[epigeal germination|epigeal]].<ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1974"/> Under swamp conditions, germination generally takes place on a sphagnum moss or a wet-muck seedbed. Seeds will not germinate under water, but some will remain viable for 30 months under water. By contrast, seeds usually fail to germinate on better drained soils because of the lack of surface water. Thus, a soil saturated but not flooded for a period of one to three months after seedfall is required for germination.<ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1965"/>

After germination, seedlings must grow fast enough to keep at least part of their crowns above floodwaters for most of the growing season.<ref>Conner, William H, 1988, Natural and artificial regeneration of baldcypress [Taxodium distichum (L.) Rich.] in the Barataria and Lake Verret basins of Louisiana. PhD Dissertation, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge. 148 p.</ref><ref>Conner, William H., and John R. Toliver. 1987. Vexar seedling protectors did not reduce nutria damage to planted baldcypress seedlings. USDA Forest Service, Tree Planter's Notes 38(3):26-29.</ref><ref>Conner, William H., John R. Toliver, and Fred H. Sklar. 1986. Natural regeneration of baldcypress [Taxodium distichum (L.) Rich.] in a Louisiana swamp. Forest Ecology and Management 14:305-317.</ref> Bald cypress seedlings can endure partial shading, but require overhead light for good growth.<ref>Williston, H. L., F. W. Shropshire, and W. E. Balmer. 1980. Cypress management: a forgotten opportunity. USDA Forest Service, Southeastern Area State and Private Forestry, Forestry Report SA-FR-8. Atlanta, GA. 8 p.</ref> Seedlings in swamps often reach heights of {{convert|20|to|75|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} their first year.<ref>Bull, H. 1949. Cypress planting in southern Louisiana. Southern Lumberman 179(2249):227-230.</ref> Growth is checked when a seedling is completely submerged by flooding, and prolonged submergence kills the seedling.<ref name="Agriculture, Forest Service 1965"/>

In nurseries, ''Taxodium distichum'' seeds show an apparent internal dormancy that can be overcome by various treatments, usually including cold stratification or submerging in water for 60 days. Nursery beds are sown in spring with pretreated seeds or in fall with untreated seeds. Seedlings usually reach {{convert|75|to|100|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in height during their first (and usually only) year in the nursery. Average size of 1-0 nursery-grown seedlings in a seed source test including 72 families was {{convert|81.4|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|1.1|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name=":4" />

Control of competing vegetation may be necessary for a year or more for bald cypress planted outside of swamps. Five years after planting on a harrowed and bedded, poorly drained site in Florida, survival was high, but heights had increased only {{convert|30|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}}, probably because of heavy herbaceous competition. Seedlings grown in a [[Crayfish|crawfish]] [[Aquaculture|pond]] in [[Louisiana]], where weed control and soil moisture were excellent through June, averaged {{convert|2.9|m|ft|abbr=on}} and {{convert|3.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} diameter at breast height after five years. However, a replicate of the same sources planted in an old soybean field, where weed control and soil moisture were poor, resulted in the same diameter, but a smaller average seedling height of {{convert|2.1|m|ft|abbr=on}}. When planted in a residential yard and weeded and watered, they averaged {{convert|3.7|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall three years later.<ref name=":4" />

===Vegetative reproduction===

Bald cypress is one of the few conifer species that sprouts. Thrifty sprouts are generally produced from stumps of young trees, but trees up to 60 years old also send up healthy sprouts if the trees are cut during the fall or winter. However, survival of these sprouts is often poor, and those that live are usually poorly shaped and do not make quality saw timber trees. Stumps of trees up to 200 years old may also sprout, but the sprouts are not as vigorous and are more subject to wind damage as the stump decays.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Coladonato |first=Milo |date=1992 |title=Taxodium ascendens, T. distichum |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/taxspp/all.html |access-date=23 October 2025 |website=Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)}}</ref> Successful vegetative propagation has been recorded when cuttings were not wounded, treated with 15,000 mg/L of [[Indole-3-butyric acid]], and grown in a substrate with intermediate water-holding capacity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=King |first=Andrew |last2=Arnold |first2=Michael |last3=Welsh |first3=Douglas |date=2011 |title=Substrates, Wounding, and Growth Regulator Concentrations Alter Adventitious Rooting of Baldcypress Cuttings |url=https://journals.ashs.org/view/journals/hortsci/46/10/article-p1387.xml |journal=HortScience |volume=46 |issue=10 |pages=1387 – 1393 |via=American Society for Horticultural Science}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Bald cypress Atchafalaya Basin.jpg|left|thumb|125px|A bald cypress in the Atchafalaya Basin of Louisiana]]
[[File:Bald cypress knees in duckweed.JPG|thumb|left|125px|Bald cypress knees in [[duckweed]]]]
The seeds remain viable for less than one year, and are dispersed in two ways. One is by water: the seeds float and move on water until flooding recedes or the cone is deposited on shore. The second is by wildlife: [[squirrel]]s eat seeds, but often drop some scales from the cones they harvest. Seeds do not germinate under water and rarely germinate on well-drained soils; seedlings normally become established on continuously saturated, but not flooded, soils for one to three months. After germination, seedlings must grow quickly to escape floodwaters; they often reach a height of 20–75 cm (up to 100 cm in fertilized [[nursery (horticulture)|nursery]] conditions) in their first year. Seedlings die if inundated for more than about two to four weeks. Natural regeneration is therefore prevented on sites that are always flooded during the growing season. Although vigorous saplings and stump sprouts can produce viable seed, most specimens do not produce seed until they are about 30 years old. In good conditions, bald cypress grows fairly fast when young, then more slowly with age. Trees have been measured to reach {{Convert|3|m|abbr=on}} in five years, {{Convert|21|m|abbr=on}} in 41 years, and {{Convert|36|m|abbr=on}} in height in 96 years; height growth has largely ceased by the time the trees are 200 years old. Some individuals can live over 1,000 years. Determination of the age of an old tree may be difficult because of frequent missing or false [[growth ring|ring]]s of stemwood caused by variable and stressful growing environments.{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

[[File:Cypress 8001.JPG|thumb|Bald cypress forest in winter, showing "knees" and (brown) high flood level, Lynches River, [[Johnsonville, South Carolina]]]]
Bald cypress trees growing in swamps have a peculiarity of growth called [[cypress knee]]s. These are woody projections from the root system project above the ground or water. Their function was once thought to be to provide [[oxygen]] to the roots, which grow in the low dissolved oxygen waters typical of a swamp (as in [[mangrove]]s). However, evidence for this is scant; in fact, roots of swamp-dwelling specimens whose knees are removed do not decrease in oxygen content and the trees continue to thrive.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} Another more likely function is structural support and stabilization. Bald cypress trees growing on flood-prone sites tend to form buttressed bases, but trees grown on drier sites may lack this feature. The buttressed base usually begins at the soil surface and usually extends up to the maximum annual flooding elevation.<ref>Pietrzykowski, M., Daniels, W. L., & Koropchak, S. C. (2015). Microtopographic effects on growth of young bald cypress (taxodium distichum L.) in a created freshwater forested wetland in southeastern Virginia. Ecological Engineering, 83, 135–143. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecoleng.2015.06.024 </ref> Buttressed bases and a strong, intertwined root system allow them to resist very strong winds; even [[hurricane]]s rarely overturn them.<ref name="Silvics" />

Many agents damage ''T. distichum'' trees. The main damaging (in some cases lethal) agent is the [[fungus]] ''Lauriliella taxodii<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.speciesfungorum.org/Names/SynSpecies.asp?RecordID=819213|title=Species Fungorum - Species synonymy|website=www.speciesfungorum.org|access-date=2019-01-21}}</ref>'', which causes a brown pocket rot known as "pecky cypress". It attacks the heartwood of living trees, usually from the crown down to the roots. A few other fungi attack the sapwood and the heartwood of the tree, but they do not usually cause serious damage. [[Insect]]s such as the cypress flea beetle (''[[Systena marginalis]]'') and the bald cypress leafroller (''[[Archips goyerana]]'') can seriously damage trees by destroying leaves, cones, or bark. [[Coypu|Nutrias]] also clip and unroot young bald cypress seedlings, sometimes killing a whole plantation in a short amount of time.<ref name="Silvics" />

In 2002, the Indiana Department of Natural Resources identified ''T. distichum'' as a state-protected plant with the status of Threatened. Globally, the species is listed as of [[Least-concern species|Least Concern]] by the [[IUCN]].{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

==Cultivation and uses==
{{More citations needed section|date=January 2021}}

[[File:Taxodium distichum02.jpg|thumb|right|{{center|Timber}}]]
The bald cypress is hardy and can be planted in hardiness zones 4 through 10 in the US or prehaps even down to USDA zone 11.<ref name="arborday.org"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=February 2022 - Baldcypress {{!}} Princeton, NJ |url=https://www.princetonnj.gov/1264/February-2022---Baldcypress |access-date=2026-06-14 |website=www.princetonnj.gov}}</ref> The species is a popular [[ornamental tree]] that is cultivated for its light, feathery foliage and orangey brown to dull red autumnal color. In cultivation it thrives on a wide range of soils, including well-drained sites where it would not grow naturally because juvenile seedlings cannot compete with other vegetation. Cultivation is successful far north of its native range, even to southern [[Canada]]. It is also commonly planted in [[Europe]], [[Asia]], and other [[temperateness|temperate]] and [[subtropical]] locales. Additionally it is sometimes planted in gardens and parks Eastern [[Australia]] with most specimens being found in Temperate to warm temperate areas although two trees are thriving in an open location along a drain on the side of the highway north of [[Port Douglas]] [[Queensland]] (the tree itself is at a latitude and longitude of-16.4853970, 145.4134609), so it would seem the species can grow well in tropical conditions. It does, however, require hot summers for good growth. 

When planted in locales with the cool summers of [[oceanic climate]]s, growth is healthy but very slow; some specimens in northeastern [[England]] have only grown to {{Convert|4-5|m|abbr=on}} tall in 50 years<ref>Tree Register of the British Isles</ref> and do not produce cones. One of the oldest specimens in [[Europe]] was planted in the 1900s in the [[Arboretum de Pézanin]] in [[Burgundy]], [[France]].  An alley of Louisiana cypress trees was planted in the 18th century in the park of the [[Château de Rambouillet]], southwest of Paris.

Bald cypress has great merchantable yields. In virgin stands, yields from 112 to 196 m<sup>3</sup>/ha were common, and some stands may have exceeded 1,000 m<sup>3</sup>/ha.


==Building material==
Still usable prehistoric wood is often found in swamps as far north as New Jersey, and occasionally as far north as Connecticut, although it is more common in the southeastern states. This partially mineralized wood is harvested from swamps in the southeastern states, and is greatly prized for special uses such as for carvings. The fungus ''Lauriliella taxodii''<ref name=":3" /> causes a specific form of the wood called "pecky cypress", which is used for decorative wall [[paneling]].

The bald cypress was used by Native Americans to create coffins, homes, drums, and canoes. [[Joshua Brown (Texas pioneer)|Joshua D. Brown]], the first settler of [[Kerrville, Texas]], made his living producing shingles from bald cypress trees that grew along the [[Guadalupe River (Texas)|Guadalupe River]] of the [[Texas Hill Country]].<ref>Texas Historical Commission, historical marker in [[Kerrville, Texas|Kerrville]], [[Texas]], 1971.</ref> 

In the southern United States, the odorless wood, which closely resembles that of other ''[[Cupressus]]'' species, has been valued since colonial times for its resistance to water, making it ideal for use wherever the wood is exposed to the elements. In the first half of the 20th century, it was marketed as "The Wood Eternal".<ref>{{cite book |title=Tidewater Red Cypress: U. S. Government Report |date=1926 |publisher=Southern Cypress Manufacturers Association |location=New Orleans |url=https://archive.org/details/TidewaterRedCypressU.s.GovernmentReportdepartmentOfAgriculture/mode/2up}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Tidewater Red Cypress |date=1920 |publisher=Florida Louisiana Red Cypress Company |location=Jacksonville, Florida |url=https://archive.org/details/buildwitharrowbr00flor/mode/2up}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=An Inside Story of Tidewater Red Cypress |date=1936 |publisher=Southern Cypress Manufacturers Association |location=Jacksonville, Florida |url=https://archive.org/details/AnInsideStoryOfTidewaterRedCypressForInteriorsOfBeautyAndStability/mode/2up |access-date=12 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=As Old as the Ark . . . As Modern as Tomorrow |date=1955 |publisher=Southern Cypress Manufacturers Association |location=Jacksonville, Florida |url=https://archive.org/details/TidewaterRedCypressAsOldAsTheArk..AsModernAsTomorrow/mode/2up |access-date=12 June 2021}}</ref>

The lumber is valuable for timber framing, building materials, fence posts, planking in boats, river pilings, doors, blinds, flooring, shingles, garden boxes, caskets, interior trim, and cabinetry.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_tadi2.pdf|website=plants.usda.gov|title=BALD CYPRESS Taxodium distichum (L.) L.C. Rich. |access-date=2019-01-14}}{{USDA}}</ref> 

Bald cypress timbers are commonly available in lengths up to 24 feet. This species enjoys predictable lead times for projects. The wood is a very light tan in color and weathers to a uniform silvery gray. Paint and stains adhere well to Bald cypress. Bald cypress most often sees use in outdoor structures such as timber frame pavilions, mid-size farmers' markets, porches, exterior awnings, and decorative trusses where its weather resistance helps ensure long life.<ref name=":0" />
